summary: RSVP-TE and its GMPLS extensions let path setup explicitly include or exclude abstract nodes and resources. This experimental RFC defines new subobjects to include or exclude autonomous systems and IGP domains in RSVP-TE signaling.

plainLanguage.summary: Telling a path-building message to travel through or avoid whole regions.

questions: what are domain subobjects in rsvp-te
how do i specify autonomous systems in rsvp-te paths
how do i exclude igp areas from rsvp-te paths
what is an explicit route object
subtitle: New subobjects for RSVP-TE to explicitly include or exclude autonomous systems and IGP domains in paths.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE allows routers to specify explicit paths including or excluding abstract nodes, but only supports 2-byte AS numbers. Modern networks use 4-byte AS numbers and need to reference routing domains like IGP areas, with no standard subobject format.
tldr.mechanism: This specification defines three new subobject types for the Explicit Route Object (ERO) and Exclude Route Object (XRO): a 4-byte AS number, an OSPF area ID, and an IS-IS area ID. These subobjects can be included in explicit routes, exclusion lists, or explicit exclusion ranges.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now build inter-domain and inter-area paths using domain-level abstractions in RSVP-TE signaling. The specification is experimental pending implementation feedback and may advance to Standards Track.

today: RFC 7898 is experimental, with a two-year evaluation period from publication. It works together with RFC 7897 (PCEP domain subobjects) to enable domain-aware path computation and signaling. The experiment remains open for feedback on implementation and deployment.

sections.title: Multi-Domain Path Setup in RSVP-TE
sections.content:
RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) and its GMPLS extensions allow a router to specify an explicit path for a traffic engineering label switched path (LSP) using abstract nodes: groups of routers whose internal topology is hidden from the ingress. RFC 3209 already defines a subobject for 2-byte AS numbers, and RFC 4874 adds route exclusion subobjects.

As networks grow and connect across multiple domains (autonomous systems and IGP areas), operators need to think in terms of these large-scale abstractions. However, RSVP-TE lacked subobject types for 4-byte AS numbers (RFC 6793 extended BGP to 4-byte ASes) and for IGP areas.

This specification adds three new subobject types to both the Explicit Route Object (ERO) and Exclude Route Object (XRO). An ERO specifies a path to include certain domains; an XRO specifies domains to avoid entirely; and an Explicit Exclusion Route Subobject (EXRS) specifies domains to avoid between specific pairs of abstract nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP-TE already lets you say 'go through this router' or 'avoid that area'. Now you can say 'go through this whole company' or 'avoid this routing region'.

sections.title: Domains and Abstract Nodes
sections.content:
A domain is any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computational responsibility. Domains include Autonomous Systems (ASes) and Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) areas.

An autonomous system is a set of routers under a single administrative domain, identified by an AS number. BGP routing operates between ASes. RFC 3209 defined a 2-byte AS subobject; RFC 6793 extended BGP to support 4-byte AS numbers, and this specification adds a 4-byte AS subobject for RSVP-TE.

An IGP area is a subdivision within an AS for routing protocols like OSPF or IS-IS. OSPF area IDs are 32-bit numbers; IS-IS area IDs are variable-length (1 to 13 octets). In both cases, the area represents a zone of routing control.

An abstract node in RSVP-TE is a domain treated as a single hop in the explicit route. The ingress router does not need to know the internal topology; it just needs to ensure the path passes through (or avoids) the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain is a group of routers you can think of as a single unit. An AS is run by one company; an area is a subdivision within that company. You can point at a domain and say 'use this' or 'skip that'.

sections.title: Subobject Encoding
sections.content:
4-Byte AS Subobject (Type 5): 8 bytes total. The L bit (loose/strict) is as defined in RFC 3209. Type is 5. Length is 8. A 2-byte Reserved field. Then the 4-byte AS number (using only the low 16 bits for 2-byte ASes, with the high 16 bits zeroed). This same format is used in both ERO and XRO; the L bit meaning differs: in ERO it is loose/strict hop; in XRO it means must-avoid (L=0) or should-avoid (L=1).

OSPF Area ID Subobject (Type 6): 8 bytes. Encodes a 32-bit OSPF area ID. Format is identical to the 4-byte AS subobject.

IS-IS Area ID Subobject (Type 7): Variable length, at least 8 bytes, multiple of 4 bytes. Includes an Area-Len field (1 to 13 octets for the actual IS-IS area identifier), followed by the variable-length area ID padded with trailing zeros to a 4-byte boundary.

These subobjects can be used in an ERO to specify an explicit route through domains, in an XRO to exclude domains globally, or in an EXRS to exclude domains between specific hops. The processing rules follow RFC 3209 (for ERO) and RFC 4874 (for XRO and EXRS).
sections.plainLanguage: Each subobject is a small block of data with a type number, a flag saying strict or loose, and the domain identifier (AS number or area ID). The format is consistent so routers always know how to interpret them.

sections.title: Mode of Operation
sections.content:
In an ERO, the new domain subobjects are treated as abstract nodes. A router receiving an ERO with an unknown subobject type (and an unrecognized Type value) follows RFC 3209 behavior: it returns a PathErr with error code 'Routing Error' and error value 'Bad EXPLICIT_ROUTE object', truncated to the offending subobject.

In an XRO, domain subobjects specify domains to exclude. A router that does not recognize a domain subobject type ignores it (as per RFC 4874), which means the desired exclusion will not be carried out. This can cause unexpected behavior in a network with mixed old and new routers.

For this reason, the experiment assumes that all nodes processing these new subobjects form part of the experiment; legacy implementations should not be mixed in.

IGP area subobjects in an XRO are local to the current AS. To exclude an area in a different AS during multi-AS path computation, the area subobject should be placed inside an EXRS within the ERO to specify the target AS.
sections.plainLanguage: When you put a domain subobject in a path specification, new routers understand it and follow it. Old routers either reject it (if it is in the explicit route) or ignore it (if it is in the exclusion). This means you need all routers to be updated for these features to work reliably.

sections.title: Practical Applications and Limitations
sections.content:
These subobjects are useful for per-domain path computation, where the full path cannot be determined at the ingress. Domain identifiers act as delimiters marking where domain boundaries start and end. For example, in an inter-AS LSP setup, an ERO might specify: (ingress-router, AS B, AS C, egress-router), leaving the detailed path within each AS to be computed by that domain's local path computation element.

The experiment is intended to run for two years after publication. At that point, the authors will assess implementation and deployment and decide whether to move to Standards Track with refinements.

The specification does not change the underlying RSVP-TE procedures for handling subobjects. It is just another tool in the operator's toolkit, alongside other mechanisms like boundary node identification. Operators may choose different approaches based on their network architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: You can use this feature to route paths through big multi-domain networks, or to avoid certain domains. The feature is experimental for two years to see if it works well in practice.
